strengths: Clear and important problem framing: demonstrates rigorously (both analytically and via simulation) that naive LLM-judge accuracy pˆ is systematically biased when the judge has imperfect sensitivity/specificity, and quantifies the direction of bias as a function of θ (Fig. 2, Sec. 4.1).

Provides a complete statistical treatment rather than just bias correction: derives a valid confidence interval accounting for two independent sources of uncertainty (test-set and calibration-set), building on established epidemiological methodology (Rogan-Gladen correction, Lang-Reiczigel CIs) but adapting it clearly to the LLM-as-judge setting with explicit formulas (Eqs. 4-7).

Introduces a genuinely useful practical contribution: an adaptive calibration-allocation algorithm (Algorithm 1) with a theoretical optimality justification (Proposition 2) that lets practitioners more efficiently spend a fixed calibration budget by allocating samples asymmetrically between 'correct' and 'incorrect' ground-truth subsets.

Thorough empirical validation via Monte Carlo simulation across a wide grid of configurations (n, m0+m1, q0, q1) in the main text and an extensive appendix (16 additional configurations), consistently showing bias reduction, near-nominal coverage, and CI-length improvements from adaptive allocation.
Provides clean, self-contained, and reproducible plug-in Python code for point estimation, CI construction, and adaptive allocation, lowering the barrier for practitioners to adopt the method.
Proofs (Propositions 1 and 2) are included and appear technically sound, giving theoretical grounding for the claimed properties rather than relying purely on empirical demonstration.
weaknesses: The core statistical machinery (Rogan-Gladen bias correction, Lang-Reiczigel confidence intervals with 'add-two-successes-two-failures' adjustment) is adapted from existing epidemiological/diagnostic-testing literature rather than newly developed; the paper's main novelty is the adaptive-allocation algorithm and its application to the LLM-judge context, which is a comparatively modest technical contribution.

All empirical validation is done via Monte Carlo simulation with hand-chosen, fixed (q0, q1) values; there is no experiment with an actual LLM judge on a real benchmark (e.g., applying the method to GPT-4-as-judge on a real dataset with human-verified calibration labels) to demonstrate practical impact on reported LLM evaluation results, which weakens the significance claims made in the introduction about correcting literature-wide evaluation bias.

The method assumes q0 and q1 are constant across the entire test distribution (i.e., judge reliability does not depend on instance difficulty, topic, or answer length); this homogeneity assumption is plausible to be violated for real LLM judges and is not discussed or tested, which could undermine the validity of the correction in practice.

The paper does not discuss the practical cost/feasibility of obtaining a human-labeled calibration dataset, which is needed for the method yet directly cuts against the 'cheap, scalable' motivation for LLM-as-judge evaluation given in the introduction; guidance on how large/representative such a calibration set needs to be in realistic settings is limited to simulation-based rules of thumb.

Limited engagement with closely related alternative approaches such as prediction-powered inference (Angelopoulos et al., 2023; Boyeau et al., 2025), which are cited in the introduction but never empirically or theoretically compared against the proposed method, leaving it unclear how this approach relates to or improves upon these alternatives.

No explicit limitations section discussing failure modes, such as small or non-representative calibration sets, potential distribution shift between calibration and test data, or extension beyond the binary correctness setting (e.g., continuous scores, multi-class judgments), which are relevant caveats for a paper whose title claims to prescribe the 'correct' way to report such evaluations.

strengths: Addresses a timely and practically important problem: naive LLM-as-a-judge accuracy estimates are biased, and the paper gives a clear, well-motivated derivation of why (Fig. 1-2, Sec. 2/4.1).

The bias-correction estimator is grounded in a classical, well-established result (Rogan-Gladen prevalence correction) and is correctly adapted with a rigorous confidence-interval construction (adjusted Wald-type interval from Lang and Reiczigel) that accounts for both test-set and calibration-set uncertainty, which prior LLM-judge discussions (Fraser, 2024; Albinet, 2025) lacked.

The adaptive calibration allocation algorithm (Algorithm 1) with a theoretically justified approximate-optimal allocation rule (Proposition 2) is a genuinely useful practical contribution that goes beyond simply invoking existing correction formulas.

Extensive Monte Carlo validation across many configurations of n, calibration size, and (q0,q1) (main text plus Appendix C) consistently confirms the theoretical claims: bias reduction, near-nominal coverage, and shorter intervals under adaptive allocation.
The paper is clearly written, well organized, and provides an accompanying plug-in Python implementation, improving reproducibility and practical adoption.
weaknesses: All empirical validation is via synthetic Monte Carlo simulation with an idealized model where q0 and q1 are constant scalars; there is no real-world case study with an actual LLM judge and human-labeled calibration set to demonstrate practical impact on genuine LLM-as-a-judge benchmarks.

The core statistical machinery (Rogan-Gladen correction, add-two-successes/failures adjusted Wald interval) is largely borrowed from classical epidemiological screening-test literature; the main originality lies in the application framing and the allocation algorithm, somewhat limiting the technical novelty.

The homogeneous-error assumption (q0, q1 constant across all instances, independent of item difficulty/domain) is a strong simplification; in practice LLM judge reliability likely varies systematically with input characteristics, which could bias the correction if unaddressed—this limitation is not explicitly discussed.

Proposition 2's optimal-allocation result relies on an approximation valid only when q0, q1 are close to 1, and its practical accuracy/robustness when judge accuracy is more moderate (e.g., 0.6-0.8) is not separately quantified beyond the simulation figures.

No sensitivity analysis or discussion of what happens when the independence assumption between test and calibration datasets is violated (e.g., calibration and test sets drawn from different distributions/domains), which is a realistic practical concern.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem statement, illustrated intuitively with Figure 1/2, showing precisely how sensitivity/specificity errors bias raw LLM-judge scores.

Provides a complete, self-contained statistical toolkit (bias-corrected point estimator, delta-method confidence interval with small-sample adjustment, and an adaptive calibration-allocation algorithm with a proven near-optimality result in Proposition 5.2) that is directly usable in practice, with accompanying plug-in Python code.

Novel theoretical contribution in Section 6 (Proposition 6.1) characterizing precisely when calibrated LLM-as-a-judge evaluation is statistically preferable to human-only evaluation, which is a useful and non-obvious framing not previously formalized in this literature.

Thorough comparison against existing bias-correction approaches (PPI, calibration-only, conditional calibration estimators) under distribution shift, showing analytically and empirically (Table 2, Figure 8) that the proposed Rogan-Gladen-based estimator uniquely remains unbiased when the marginal label distribution differs between test and calibration sets, a realistic practical concern.

Extensive empirical validation combining controlled Monte Carlo simulations (with coverage and interval-length checks across many parameter settings, Appendix J) and real-world validation on Chatbot Arena and AlpacaEval across seven contemporary LLM judges, including ranking-recovery analysis (Appendix K) showing practical impact on model rankings.

Honest and transparent reporting of limitations, including the fact that none of the evaluated real LLM judges currently fall within the variance-favorable regime on Chatbot Arena, and clear articulation of the assumptions required for validity (e.g., invariance of judge behavior across test/calibration sets).
weaknesses: The core statistical machinery (Rogan-Gladen prevalence correction, delta-method variance, 'add-two-successes-two-failures' Wald interval) is adapted from pre-existing epidemiology/screening-test literature (Rogan & Gladen, 1978; Lang & Reiczigel, 2014) rather than newly derived; the paper's novelty lies mainly in the LLM-judge framing, the adaptive allocation algorithm, and the variance-regime/distribution-shift analyses, making the core methodological contribution somewhat incremental.

The framework assumes a single global sensitivity/specificity pair (q0, q1) that is homogeneous across the test population, independent of covariates such as prompt difficulty, response length, or style; this is acknowledged only briefly in the limitations/appendix rather than empirically probed, despite prior work (e.g., length bias in LLM judges) suggesting such heterogeneity is common and could undermine the invariance assumption central to the paper's bias-correction and distribution-shift-robustness claims.

The distribution-shift robustness result relies on a fairly specific assumption (only the marginal label distribution Pr(Z) shifts while the conditional judge behavior Pr(Ẑ|Z) is exactly invariant across P and Q); more realistic shifts where judge behavior itself changes with covariates are only mentioned as future work, limiting the practical scope of the 'robust under distribution shift' claim.

The real-data demonstration that calibrated LLM-as-a-judge evaluation can beat human-only evaluation (Section 6) is not actually realized for any of the seven contemporary judges tested on Chatbot Arena (Figure 6), somewhat weakening the practical significance of this contribution, even though this is honestly reported.

The multi-category extension (Appendix B) is validated only on a small synthetic simulation rather than real multi-category/rating-scale evaluation data, leaving its practical applicability (e.g., for Likert-scale or review-style scoring) less thoroughly demonstrated than the binary case.

Real-world empirical validation is limited to a relatively small set of models/pairs from Chatbot Arena and AlpacaEval; broader benchmarks or tasks (e.g., open-ended generation quality, reasoning correctness) are not explored, leaving some uncertainty about generalizability across evaluation domains.

strengths: Addresses a timely and practically important problem: the systematic reporting of LLM-as-a-judge scores without accounting for judge sensitivity/specificity, which the paper convincingly shows induces predictable bias.

The theoretical development is careful and largely rigorous: closed-form bias characterization, an unbiased/asymptotically-corrected estimator, a delta-method-based confidence interval accounting for both test- and calibration-set uncertainty, and formal propositions (with proofs in the appendix) establishing bias reduction, optimal calibration allocation, and conditions under which LLM-judge evaluation beats human-only evaluation.

The comparison in Table 1 and Figure 5, showing that the proposed misclassification-adjusted estimator remains unbiased under label-distribution shift between test and calibration sets (unlike calibration-only, difference, or conditional-calibration estimators), is a genuinely useful and non-trivial contribution relevant to real deployment scenarios where calibration sets are curated differently from test sets.

Extensive empirical validation: Monte Carlo simulations across many (n, m, q0, q1) configurations (main text and appendix) confirm bias reduction and near-nominal coverage, and a real-world validation on Chatbot Arena with six models and a GPT-4.1-mini judge shows consistent bias reduction and good coverage across repeated random splits.

Practical, low-friction proposal: requires only a modest calibration set and provides a simple plug-in formula/code (Appendix C), making adoption straightforward for practitioners currently reporting raw LLM-judge accuracies.
Clear writing and good use of illustrative figures (e.g., Figure 1, 2, 4) that build intuition about the bias mechanism and the framework's advantages.
weaknesses: The core statistical machinery (Rogan-Gladen correction, Lang-Reiczigel confidence interval with the add-two-successes/failures adjustment) is adapted from classical epidemiological/screening-test literature rather than newly derived; the paper's novel contributions are comparatively narrower (adaptive calibration allocation, human-vs-LLM variance comparison, and the distribution-shift robustness argument), making the overall originality more incremental than transformative.

The framework assumes a binary correct/incorrect judgment and a confusion matrix Pr(Ẑ|Z) that is stable across test and calibration distributions; it does not address dependence on auxiliary factors ξ (e.g., response length, style, self-preference bias) that are well documented to affect LLM judges in practice—this is deferred entirely to future work despite being central to real-world judge reliability.

Extension to multinomial/graded judgments (e.g., Likert-scale or pairwise preference with ties), which is common in practice, is left as future work, limiting immediate applicability to many real evaluation setups.

The real-world validation (Chatbot Arena) is relatively limited in scope: a single judge model (GPT-4.1-mini), six response models, and no head-to-head empirical comparison against alternative bias-correction methods (PPI, difference estimator, conditional calibration) on real data—such comparisons are only done via simulation (Figure 5), leaving open how large the practical benefit is on real, noisy human-labeled data.

Practical guidance on calibration-budget requirements when the judge is only moderately reliable (q close to 0.5) is acknowledged theoretically (Proposition 5.1) but not empirically explored with realistic LLM judges whose sensitivity/specificity may be far from the near-perfect regime assumed in several propositions (e.g., Proposition 5.2 assumes q̃0, q̃1 close to 1).

strengths: Addresses a timely and practically important problem: naive reporting of LLM-as-a-judge scores is statistically biased, and the paper provides a simple, principled fix grounded in classical epidemiological misclassification theory (Rogan & Gladen).

The theoretical development is thorough and rigorous: closed-form bias expressions, an asymptotic variance derivation via the delta method, a small-sample adjusted Wald confidence interval, and formal propositions (with proofs in the appendix) characterizing (i) when the bias-corrected estimator dominates the naive estimator in bias, (ii) the optimal calibration-label allocation to minimize CI length, and (iii) precise parameter regimes where LLM-as-a-judge with correction beats human-only evaluation in variance.

The distribution-shift analysis in Section 8 is a genuine and useful contribution: it clarifies the differing implicit invariance assumptions behind existing bias-correction estimators (naive, calibration-only, PPI-style difference estimator, conditional calibration estimator) via a unified table, and shows both theoretically and empirically that only the misclassification-adjusted (Rogan-Gladen-style) estimator remains unbiased when calibration and test label marginals differ, a realistic scenario in practice given how calibration sets are typically curated.

Reasonably comprehensive empirical validation combining controlled Monte Carlo experiments (bias, CI coverage, CI length, multiple q0/q1/m/n configurations reported in the appendix) with a real-world validation on Chatbot Arena across six models and an actual LLM judge (GPT-4.1-mini), showing consistent bias reduction and near-nominal coverage.

Practical usability: the paper provides a plug-in Python implementation (point_estimator/confidence_interval functions shown in the appendix) that is simple to adopt, and the adaptive calibration allocation algorithm gives actionable guidance for practitioners on how to budget human annotation effort.
Clear exposition with intuitive visual aids (Figure 1-2 sequence) that build up the bias problem and its correction in an accessible way despite the underlying statistics being somewhat technical.
weaknesses: The core statistical machinery (Rogan-Gladen correction, adjusted Wald intervals à la Lang & Reiczigel, delta-method variance) is directly imported from existing epidemiology/diagnostic-testing literature; the paper's novelty is primarily in application/repackaging to the LLM-judge setting plus the allocation algorithm and the distribution-shift argument, which is a comparatively incremental theoretical contribution despite being well-executed.

The core method assumes a single scalar sensitivity/specificity pair (q0, q1) for the LLM judge that is constant across the test distribution; real LLM judges are known to have systematic, correlated biases (e.g., length bias, position bias, style bias) that could make q0/q1 vary with covariates ξ, and this important complication is deferred entirely to 'future work' rather than empirically explored, even briefly, in the current experiments.

The empirical validation, while present, is somewhat narrow: the real-data validation is limited to a single dataset (Chatbot Arena) with a single judge model (GPT-4.1-mini) and relatively small held-out calibration splits (10%); no comparison against modern PPI variants (PPI++, cross-prediction-powered inference) is shown empirically even though these are discussed and cited as close competitors, leaving the claimed advantage over PPI-style methods only partially substantiated in real-world settings (only shown via a synthetic shift experiment in Fig. 7).

The paper does not empirically explore how the method scales/degrades when q0 and q1 themselves are estimated with very small calibration budgets (e.g., very few positive or negative examples) or when the judge's sensitivity/specificity is close to the boundary q0+q1=1, where the estimator becomes numerically unstable (correction denominator approaches zero); this is a known failure mode of Rogan-Gladen-type estimators that deserves more explicit discussion/guardrails beyond passing mention.

Proposition 6.1's practical relevance requires q to be fairly high (>~0.85, since q1 in the stated range 1/2+1/(2√2)≈0.854) for the human-only vs. LLM-judge variance comparison to yield a real-valued informative regime, and the simplifying assumption q0=q1 in several propositions (5.1, 6.1) may not hold for many actual judges observed in practice (e.g., the Chatbot Arena experiment itself has visibly different bias directions per model, suggesting asymmetric q0 vs q1), somewhat limiting the direct applicability of the cleanest theoretical guarantees.

Minor presentation issues: some notation is dense and introduced across multiple sections (e.g., tilde vs hat quantities in Section 4.2), which could challenge readers less familiar with the misclassification-correction literature; also, while an anonymized code repository is referenced, its accessibility/completeness cannot be fully verified from the submission alone.
